titre: Pauli's 1930 Letter: A Particle Proposed as a Last Resort
accroche: On December 4, 1930, Pauli proposes a particle he calls the “neutron” and misses the meeting to go to a ball. It will not be detected until 1956.
contenu_vulgarise:
On December 4, 1930, Wolfgang Pauli writes from Zurich to physicists gathered in Tübingen. The letter begins with “Dear radioactive ladies and gentlemen” and ends with an excuse: he will not come, he is “indispensable” in Zurich for a ball, on the night of December 6 to 7. In between, he proposes a new particle.

## A Desperate Remedy

The problem is that of the continuous spectrum of beta decay. A nucleus emits an electron, but the electron's energy is not always the same, and not all the lost energy is recovered. Pauli speaks of a “desperate remedy” to save both the law of conservation of energy and the “exchange theorem” of statistics, which the nuclei of nitrogen and lithium-6 also threaten.

His idea: there would exist in nuclei electrically neutral particles, of spin 1/2, that obey the exclusion principle and do not travel at the speed of light. He calls them “neutrons.” Emitted with the electron, they would carry off the missing energy, so that the sum of the two is constant. Their mass would be on the order of the electron's and should in any case not exceed 0.01 times that of the proton.

Pauli concedes that his remedy may seem unbelievable: if these particles existed, they would have been seen long ago. He also quotes a remark by Peter Debye, heard in Brussels: better not to think about it, like the new taxes. The text preserved in English is an abridged version of the original, notes the Royal Holloway university page that reproduces it.

## A Name That Changes Hands

Two years later, James Chadwick discovers a neutral particle in the nucleus, much more massive, and it is christened the “neutron.” Pauli's particle needs another name. Fermi calls it the “neutrino,” the little neutral one. Sources diverge on the date: the Wikipedia article cites a conference in Paris in July 1932 and the Solvay congress of October 1933, whereas the Royal Holloway page mentions a seminar in 1934. That page adds that Pauli judged his hypothesis too speculative to publish in a journal before 1934.

## More Than Twenty-Five Years Later

On July 20, 1956, *Science* publishes “Detection of the Free Neutrino: a Confirmation,” signed by Clyde Cowan, Frederick Reines, and three colleagues. Their detector, placed near a nuclear reactor at the Savannah River Plant, in South Carolina, 11 meters from the reactor and 12 meters underground, records about three neutrino interactions per hour. These are antineutrinos, coming from the reactor.

## Inventor, Not Discoverer

Pauli is often presented as the discoverer of the neutrino. He is its inventor, in the sense that he invented a particle without being able to see it. And he invented it so that the conservation of energy would remain true. This choice, keeping a principle by accepting an entity that no one sees, held for more than twenty-five years before being confirmed.

At what point does an entity postulated to save a principle cease to be a contrivance?

repere.texte: Letter of December 4, 1930: Pauli proposes neutral particles of spin 1/2, which he calls “neutrons,” whose mass should not exceed 0.01 proton mass. Cowan and Reines publish their detection in Science on July 20, 1956, twenty-five years and seven months later.
repere.source: Royal Holloway, abridged translation of Pauli's letter; Cowan et al., Science 124 (3212), 103-104, 1956

carte.punch: Pauli proposed a particle in 1930, as a “desperate remedy.” Seen in 1956.
carte.idee: Pauli calls it “neutron” and invents it to save the conservation of energy in beta decay. Chadwick discovers a different neutron in 1932, and Fermi renames the particle neutrino. Cowan and Reines detect it near a reactor in 1956.

quiz.question: Why does Pauli propose, in 1930, the existence of a neutral particle emitted with the electron?
choix: To explain why nuclei are stable despite the repulsion between protons
To save the conservation of energy in beta decay, whose spectrum is continuous
To predict the particle that Chadwick discovers two years later
To interpret an unknown particle observed in cosmic rays
quiz.explication: Pauli proposes a desperate remedy to save the conservation of energy in the face of the continuous spectrum of beta decay. The stability of nuclei is a different question. Chadwick's neutron is another particle, much more massive. And nothing had been observed in cosmic rays: confirmation comes in 1956, at a reactor.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What name does Pauli give, in his 1930 letter, to the particle he proposes?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Pauli calls his particle the neutron in 1930; it is Fermi who renames it the neutrino after Chadwick discovers, in 1932, another neutron far more massive.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why does Pauli not attend the Tübingen meeting where his letter is read?
choix: He is ill and cannot travel
He judges the meeting to be of no scientific interest
He has to stay in Zurich for a ball, on December 6 and 7
He is preparing the publication of his discovery
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Pauli writes that he is indispensable in Zurich for a ball on the night of December 6 to 7, 1930; the letter mentions neither illness nor lack of interest.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who detects Pauli's particle, and where?
choix: Cowan and Reines, near a nuclear reactor, in 1956
Chadwick, in the atomic nucleus, in 1932
Fermi, at the Paris conference, in 1932
Lee and Yang, at Columbia University, in 1956
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Cowan and Reines publish their detection in Science in July 1956, with a detector installed near the reactor of the Savannah River Plant, in South Carolina.
